title: Architecture & Standards — Integrated Guidelines and ADR Process
author: Asha Patel
body:
Purpose
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It also documents the ADR (Architectural Decision Record) process and provides concrete rules, templates, and examples teams must follow for production services.

Scope
Applies to all services, SDKs, deployment artifacts, and infra managed by Redwood Inference (hosted, dedicated, private). Exceptions require an approved ADR.

1) API standards
Overview
Our APIs must be stable, discoverable, and easy to use for internal teams and external customers. Follow OpenAPI-first design for HTTP APIs and protobuf/gRPC for internal high-throughput links.
Key rules
- Versioning: All public APIs must include a major version in the base path (e.g., /v1/). Major version bumps are allowed for incompatible changes only. Minor/patch changes must be backward compatible.
- Contract: Ship an OpenAPI v3 spec for every public endpoint and publish it in our API catalog. Specs must include request/response schemas, examples, error responses, and auth requirements.
- Error model: Use a consistent error envelope: {"code": string, "message": string, "details": optional object}. HTTP status codes: 200 (OK), 202 (Accepted for async), 400 (Bad request), 401, 403, 404, 409 (conflict), 429 (rate limit), 500 (internal).
- Idempotency: For any non-idempotent operation, expose an Idempotency-Key header and persist idempotency state for 24 hours.
- Pagination: Use cursor-based pagination for large result sets; avoid offset pagination for production endpoints.
- Rate limiting: Document per-route limits in the OpenAPI spec. Implement token bucket enforcement at the gateway.
- Deprecation policy: Mark deprecated endpoints in the OpenAPI spec and follow a minimum 90-day deprecation window for public APIs; notify downstream teams and add telemetry that surfaces deprecated usage.
API Design checklist (PR required)
1. OpenAPI spec included in /specs/ with examples.
2. Integration tests that validate contract (schema + example flows).
3. Backward compatibility test (if not a major version).
4. Documentation page in the internal API catalog.
Example: error envelope
```json
{
  "code": "model_not_ready",
  "message": "The requested model is currently loading",
  "details": {"estimated_ready_seconds": 12}
}
```

2) Coding standards
Supported languages: Go (services/runtime), Python (evaluation, infra automation), TypeScript (console & SDKs).
General rules
- Formatting & linters: enable gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, black + ruff + mypy for Python, and eslint + prettier + TypeScript strict for TS. PRs must pass CI linting before merge.
- Tests: Unit tests required; aim for >= 70% coverage for service packages. Critical path code (auth, routing, model I/O) must have >= 90% coverage and mutation tests where practical.
- Type safety: Enable static typing where language supports it (mypy, TypeScript strict).
- Secrets: Never commit secrets in code. Use runtime secrets (Vault/KMS) and local .env.example for development.
- Naming: Use clear, domain-driven identifiers. Public API fields should be snake_case for JSON payloads. Internal Go/TS identifiers should follow language conventions.
CI pipeline requirements
- Unit tests, integration tests (if included in repo), linting, license scanning, SCA (software composition analysis).
- PR template must include risk category, rollout plan, and required reviewers (service owners + infra).

3) Infrastructure standards
IaC and environment separation
- Terraform is the canonical IaC. Use the /terraform/modules pattern and shared modules published to the internal module registry. No ad-hoc cloud resources outside Terraform without an ADR.
- Environments: dev, staging, prod. Network isolation between environments (VPC-per-env or subnet segregation) and least-privilege IAM roles.
- Tagging: All cloud resources must include tags: team, service, env, owner, cost-center.
Secrets & keys
- KMS-backed encryption for all persistent secrets. KMS keys must be rotated at least annually. Use Vault for runtime secrets retrieval.
Networking
- Allow-lists: egress and ingress must be explicit for prod services. Bastion/access proxies required for management plane access.
Observability & ownership
- Each service must have: metrics emitting (Prometheus style), structured logs (json), and traces (OpenTelemetry). Owners register dashboards and SLOs in the central observability repo.
Policy as code
- Use Sentinel/OPA policies enforced in CI to validate terraform plans for approved regions, instance types, and public networking.
Example Terraform module use (snippet)
```hcl
module "vpc" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@internal.module.registry/terraform/aws/vpc.git//modules/primary"
  team = "inference-runtime"
  env  = var.env
}
```

4) Model-serving standards
Model metadata and onboarding
- Model card: Every model must include a model card (YAML) with: model_id, architecture, tokenizer, quantization_profile, training_data_summary, expected failure modes, evaluation prompts, and privacy considerations. Store model cards in the model-catalog repo.
- Versioning: Adopt semantic model versions: <model_id>@vMAJOR.MINOR (e.g., redwood-13b@v2.1). The model registry holds artifacts and checksums.
Runtime & configuration
- Quantization profiles: Document supported quantization profiles (e.g., int8, int4, nf4) in quantization-profiles/ and test for quality regressions with the eval-harness.
- KV cache consistency: For multi-node serving, ensure KV cache is warm during scale-up via prefetch jobs. Define cache-warming windows in deployment manifests.
Deployment and rollout
- Canary: Default canary rollout for model changes: 5% for 30 minutes, 20% for 1 hour, 100% if no errors. Abort on >1% error increase or p95 latency increase >20%.
- Rollback: Automatic rollback if thresholds breached. Rollback must be executed within 10 minutes of detection for public endpoints.
- Compatibility: If serving older model variants as fallbacks, ensure API contract compatibility and add health-checks that validate output shape.
Quality gates
- All model onboarding requires: automated evals vs. canonical prompt-sets, A/B regressions vs. baseline, and perf benchmarks (p50/p95 latency under expected batch sizes).

5) Observability standards
Metric taxonomy
- Use consistent metric names: service_{component}_{action}_duration_ms (histogram), service_{component}_errors_total (counter), service_{component}_requests_total (counter). Include labels: service, env, region, model_id, route.
Tracing and logs
- OpenTelemetry for traces. Sample rates: default 10% for non-prod, 100% for traces hitting rate-limited errors or high-severity alerts. Logs must be JSON, include trace_id, span_id, request_id, user_id (when available).
Dashboards & SLOs
- SLOs: Define one availability SLO and one latency SLO per public route. SLO template:
  - Availability: >= 99.9% over 30 days (error = 5xx + 429 where rate limit not expected).
  - Latency: p95 <= route-specific target (see performance section).
- Alerting: Pager duty for P1 (SLO burn rate > 2x for 1 hour) and channel alert for P2. All alerts must include runbook links and owner.
Synthetic tests
- Baseline synthetic tests per route executed every 2 minutes from multiple regions. Results feed into canary analysis for deploys.

6) Performance standards and benchmarking
Latency & throughput targets
- Host API (text generation): p50 <= 40ms per token, p95 <= 200ms per token for small models on dedicated infra. Public endpoints should specify route-level targets.
- Embeddings: p50 <= 60ms, p95 <= 300ms for typical batch sizes (<= 32).
- Throughput: Provide expected throughput per SKU in the model catalog (tokens/sec per GPU type).
Benchmarking process
- Use the benchmarking-and-perf-suite repo. Every significant change to the runtime or model (quantization, kernel change) gets a bench run comparing p50/p95/throughput and memory/KV behaviour.
- Thresholds: Any change that increases p95 by >10% or reduces throughput by >15% requires a rollback plan and an ADR if accepted.
Load testing
- Load tests should run in staging using realistic traffic profiles and include cache/cold-start scenarios. Define traffic mix based on real production traces sampled via observability.

7) ADR (Architectural Decision Record) process
What is an ADR?
- An ADR records important architectural decisions and their context. Use the ADR template for decisions that affect cross-team compatibility, infra, or long-lived tradeoffs.
When to write an ADR
- Introducing new infra components (e.g., switching to a new scheduler), changing API versioning strategies, adopting a new model serialization format, or approving exceptions to standards.
ADR template (use plain text or markdown)
- Title: short descriptive title
- Status: proposed | accepted | superseded | deprecated
- Context: problem and constraints
- Decision: chosen approach and rationale
- Consequences: migration steps, risks, and follow-ups
- Owners and reviewers
How to submit
1. Create ADR markdown in the /adrs/ directory of the architecture repo. File name: YYYYMMDD-title.md.
2. Open an RFC PR and tag owner teams and reviewers.
3. Allow 7 business days for review. For urgent decisions, include an accelerated path and record quorum.
4. Upon merge, update the ADR index and link related implementation tickets.
Examples of recent ADRs
- 20250601-protobuf-for-internal-service-payloads.md (accepted): rationale: compactness, forward compatibility, and fast gRPC behaviour.
- 20251015-unified-model-card-spec.md (accepted): established the YAML model-card schema and required fields.

8) Governance, exceptions, and compliance
- Exceptions: All deviations from these standards must have an ADR with explicit time-bound approvals and mitigation plans.
- Security & compliance: Security reviews required for changes impacting data plane, encryption, or customer data flow. See sec-review checklist.
- Ownership: Each service must list a primary owner and on-call rotation in the service manifest. Owners are responsible for SLOs, runbooks, and pager coverage.

Appendices
A. Example PR checklist
- Link to OpenAPI spec: yes/no
- Unit tests: yes/no
- Integration tests: yes/no
- Load test (if perf-sensitive): yes/no
- Lint & formatting: pass/fail
- ADR required: yes/no
- Rollout plan and monitoring: included

B. API naming quick reference
- Base path: /v{MAJOR}/{service}/{resource}
- Resource names: plural nouns (e.g., /v1/models, /v1/requests)
- Use HTTP verbs for actions; avoid RPC-like verbs in paths when possible.

C. Contact & ownership
- Architecture guild: architecture@redwood-inference.internal (subscribe for ADR announcements)
- Standards steward: Asha Patel (owner), backups: Evelyn Zhao, Liam O'Connor
